title: Writing in public changes the reading.
dek: My review kept 752 words of a book I estimate at 90.000 words - about one word for every 120 read. Knowing you will explain a book changes what you read it for, and not only for the better.
whyThisIdea: Este prima idee din backlog care nu a fost amânată (#23), iar după 63 de zile de la primul articol e momentul bun să vorbești despre cum blogul ți-a schimbat cititul. Se leagă de „A note is not a recording” și „Books finished is the wrong number”, dar unghiul e nou: publicul, nu ritmul sau notițele.

entry.title: Writing in public changes the reading.
entry.titleHtml: Writing in public changes the reading.
entry.dek: My review kept 752 words of a book I estimate at 90.000 words - about one word for every 120 read. Knowing you will explain a book changes what you read it for, and not only for the better.
body: “You read a book differently when you know somebody will ask you what was in it.”

Have you ever asked yourself if you read a book the same way when you know you will have to talk about it afterwards? Today is Wednesday, the 18th of November, and it has been 63 days since the 16th of September, the day the first article went up on this site. Somewhere in those 63 days I noticed something I did not plan for. The blog did not only change how much I write. It changed how I read. So the question is: is that a good thing, or did I just turn every book into homework? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at is reading with an audience in your head, and I met it in my own room, with a pencil in my hand. Before this blog, reading was simple. I opened the book, I read until I was tired, I closed it, and maybe I told a friend one thing I liked. Now there is a second voice while I read, and it keeps asking the same question: “would this make it into the article?”. Some pages get a line under them. Some pages get a number in the margin that I want to check later. And some pages, if I am honest, get nothing, because the voice already decided they will not be useful.

Firstly, let’s split the idea in two, the way I like to do. “Writing” and “in public”. The writing part I already talked about in my article about notes - a note is a decision about what matters, not a copy of everything. Writing about a book is the same decision, only bigger. The second half, “in public”, is the one that changed me more. When I write only for myself, I can be vague. I can write “compound interest is important” and I know what I meant. When somebody else reads it, “I know what I meant” is not enough anymore. Every number has to be checked, because somebody can check it. Every claim has to be explained, because nobody is inside my head. <u>Writing for yourself, you can be vague. Writing in public, vague becomes visible.</u>

Secondly, let’s do the arithmetic, because this is the part that surprised me. My review of “The Psychology of Money” has 752 words (I counted them). Let’s say the book has 300 pages and every page has 300 words - these two numbers are my assumption, not a measurement, books are very different.
Words in the book: 300 × 300 = 90.000
Words read for every word I wrote: 90.000 ÷ 752 = 119.7

So for every 120 words I read, I could keep about one. That is 0.84% of the book that survives into the article, and 99.16% that stays behind. And this changes everything about how you read. If I can keep almost nothing, I cannot read for everything anymore. I start reading for the 1% - the idea that holds the others together, the example that explains it best, the line I would put at the top. <u>When you know you can keep less than 1%, every page has to fight for its place.</u> Reading turns into choosing, and choosing is a much more active thing than turning pages.

And this is not only my feeling. In 2014, a group of psychologists led by John Nestojko at Washington University in St. Louis published a study with a very honest title: “Expecting to teach enhances learning and organization of knowledge in free recall of text passages”. Some people read a text knowing they would be tested on it. Others read the same text believing they would have to teach it to another student afterwards. Here is the interesting part - nobody actually taught anything. In the end, everybody got the same test. And the people who expected to teach remembered more of the text, organized what they remembered better, and answered more questions correctly, especially about the main points. Only the expectation of explaining it was enough to change the reading. For me, this blog is exactly that expectation, every week, and you are the student I am preparing for (thank you).

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. Reading for the article has a cost, and I can already see it. When the article is the goal, the book becomes material. I catch myself looking for the line that sounds good as an epigraph, not the line that is most true. I like the chapters that give me a number I can calculate, because a calculation makes a good “Secondly”. And the chapters that do not fit - I read them faster. In my review of “The Psychology of Money” I wrote that I did not enjoy the graphs and the stories about the 1920s and 1930s. I still think some of them could be shorter. But now I also ask myself: did I not enjoy them, or did they simply not fit in 752 words? <u>A book read for an article can lose exactly the parts that do not fit in the article.</u> There is a second cost too. I notice that I look at a new book and, before opening it, I already ask “can I write about this?”. A book that is hard to explain is not a worse book. It is just a harder article.

So here is what I am going to try. One, I write about a book only a few days after I finish it, and without opening it again while I write - so what goes into the article is what actually stayed, not what I underlined. Two, one book every now and then is just for me. No pencil, no margin, no voice asking about the article. If I want to talk about it later, fine, but I am not allowed to decide that before the last page.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I really believe that writing in public made me a better reader than I was in all my years of school. I finish books, I check the numbers, I remember the main idea weeks later, and the study above says this is not only in my head. But I have to be honest about two things. 63 days and two book reviews are not enough to know if this lasts, or if it is just the excitement of something new. And I think I lost something real - reading for nothing, just because a book is good, without asking what it is useful for. Not every book should become content. What I take from it is simple: read as if you will explain it, but do not read only for the explanation.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“You read a book differently when you know somebody will ask you what was in it.”
